<main class="site-main"><section class="page-intro"><p class="section-number">Article · Evidence and belief</p><h1>Rejecting the null hypothesis or not?</h1><div class="article-meta"><span class="status">in bloom</span><span>04 Sep 2023</span></div></section><article class="prose"><p>A p-value can look like a small, clean answer. The trouble begins when different interpretations of probability ask it to answer different questions.</p><h2>The puzzle</h2><p>Under a null model, how surprising is data at least as extreme as the data observed? That is a useful calculation. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.</p><h2>Why the paradox matters</h2><p>Fisherian testing, Neyman–Pearson decision rules, and Bayesian inference organize uncertainty differently. The same observed result can therefore support different next steps, depending on the question and the model.</p><blockquote>Do not ask a number to answer a question it was not built to answer.</blockquote><p>This is a theory note with a practical ending: state the estimand, state the decision rule, and show the model that connects the data to the conclusion.</p></article></main>
